newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Van Miert slams Boeing exclusive supply deals.
newsitem.headline: Van Miert slams Boeing exclusive supply deals.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert made it clear during a trip to the United States this week that he is unhappy with Boeing Co's exclusive sales agreements with U.S. airlines.
The U.S. aircraft manufacturer has struck exclusive provider relationships with Delta Air Lines Inc and AMR Corp's American Airlines.
"As far as the exclusive agreements are concerned, I can't see any solution. We have to take a negative view on that. Exclusive agreements are out of the question.", he said in Atlanta on Wednesday.
The Commission a month ago launched a full probe of Boeing's proposed merger with McDonnell Douglas, which would create the world's largest aerospace conglomerate.

Van Miert, speaking to reporters after a meeting with business leaders, said he would discuss the planned merger with U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno and U.S. antitrust officials on Thursday and Friday.
He said he would also meet AMR Chief Executive Robert Crandall in Washington. Asked what his message on Boeing would be, he responded: "We have a big problem. There is a real big problem."

Van Miert told the Belgian-American Chamber of Commerce during a luncheon speech that Boeing already dominated Europe with a 60 percent market share, while Boeing and McDonnell Douglas together accounted for 80 percent of the airliners currently in service.
He said the merger also had competitive ramifications for the European defense industry.
"I have the intent to raise this in Washington during my visit," he said.

Van Miert criticized Boeing's exclusive aircraft purchase deals with American and Delta, as well as the possibility of a similar deal with Continental Airlines Inc. "This is absolutely flying in the face of basic rules concerning competition policy...therefore, I have to make it perfectly clear that we certainly are not going to accept it, not within the framework of the merger or even outside the merger," he said.
"It would lead to a situation where a big part of the market was closed, not just for a few years but for 15 or 20. This kind of practice cannot be accepted at all."
He told a questioner that if an exclusive sales agreement between Boeing and a U.S. airline were ruled anti-competitive by European authorities, action could be taken against the airline.
"That means (the company's) activities within the European market would be illegal, with all the consequences. Another possibility would be to impose fines," Van Miert said.
But he emphasized that the EU was most concerned about Boeing and its role as arch-rival to the European aircraft manufacturing consortium, Airbus Industrie.
